text:
Richard Stallman, born March 16, 1953, is a pioneering figure in the free software movement. A self-taught programmer, he became a central figure in the hacker culture at MIT, advocating for unrestricted access to computer source code. His 1983 announcement of the GNU project aimed to create a free operating system compatible with Unix, emphasizing the freedom to share, study, and modify software. Stallman founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 to support this philosophy, introducing the concept of copyleft to protect the rights of software users. He developed foundational tools like GNU Emacs, GCC, and GNU Make, and his advocacy led to the creation of the GNU General Public License (GPL), which ensures software remains free.
Stallman’s activism has been marked by his opposition to proprietary software, digital rights management (DRM), and surveillance. His work has inspired the open-source movement, though he prefers the term "free software" to highlight its ethical and moral dimensions. Despite controversies, including debates over his views on underage sex and his 2019 resignation from MIT and FSF, Stallman remains a vocal advocate for software freedom, influencing global debates on intellectual property, privacy, and technological access. His contributions have left a lasting impact on computing and digital rights.
